item.title: Medicare Advantage’s Audit Crackdown Could Reach the Strip Center
item.dc:creator: Travis Barrington
item.description:
A proposed CMS audit rule targets Medicare Advantage upcoding, pressuring insurer-owned senior clinics that retail and medical office landlords have courted as tenants.

The post Medicare Advantage’s Audit Crackdown Could Reach the Strip Center appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
For the past several years, few tenants looked better on a shopping center rent roll than a senior primary care clinic. They sign long leases, invest heavily in their space, bring steady daytime traffic and are often backed by some of the largest health insurers in the country. A rule proposed this week in Washington is a reminder that the business model behind many of those leases runs on federal payment formulas, and those formulas are being rewritten.

On Nov. 16, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services proposed a sweeping anti-fraud rule it calls CRUSH, short for Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare. CMS says the rule would save nearly $90 billion over the next decade across Medicare, Medicaid and the ACA marketplace. The provision that matters most for insurers would revive a version of the agency’s 2023 risk adjustment data validation (RADV) rule, letting CMS extrapolate audit findings from a sample of enrollees across an entire Medicare Advantage contract, going back to payment year 2018. According to Becker’s Hospital Review, CMS estimates the change would let it recover about $9 billion a year in overpayments.

Health insurer shares fell sharply on Wednesday as investors weighed the proposal. Humana dropped 12.98%, UnitedHealth Group fell 10.21% and Elevance Health lost 7.63%. Most of the coverage has focused on what the rule means for insurer earnings. Much less attention has gone to the buildings where Medicare Advantage care is actually delivered, and to the landlords who own them.

Why insurers built clinics

Medicare Advantage, the privately run alternative to traditional Medicare, now covers more than half of all Medicare beneficiaries. Enrollment is concentrated at the top: UnitedHealth and Humana together account for 46% of Medicare Advantage enrollees, according to KFF. As the program grew, insurers moved aggressively into owning the doctors’ offices where their members get care.

A study by researchers at the Brookings Institution and Cornell, published in Health Affairs Scholar, found that payer-operated practices accounted for 4.2% of the national Medicare primary care market by service volume in 2023, up from 0.8% in 2016. UnitedHealth’s Optum was the largest, with more than 2.7% of the national market and over 35% in several large counties. Insurers were significantly more likely to own practices where Medicare Advantage enrollment was high, and more than 15% of Americans lived in counties where payers owned over 10% of the primary care market.

Humana built the most visible senior-focused network. Its CenterWell and Conviva brands operated more than 340 primary care centers at the end of 2024, up from roughly 200 at the start of 2022, including clinics co-located with Walmart stores, Healthcare Dive reported. In February, executives said they planned to add up to 70 more clinics in 2026. Humana has since formed a joint venture with BlackRock’s HPS Investment Partners covering nearly 150 CenterWell clinics.

The coding question

The economics of these clinics are tied to how Medicare Advantage pays. Plans receive more money for members who are documented as sicker. Brookings’ Loren Adler has suggested insurers may be expanding their practice networks partly to increase upcoding, the practice of coding enrollees as sicker than they are to raise federal payments. The study did not prove that link, but earlier research has found that vertically integrated insurers code their members more intensely. MedPAC estimates upcoding accounts for almost half of the roughly $84 billion in extra payments Medicare Advantage plans received in 2025.

That is what CMS is now targeting from several directions. In January, the agency’s proposed 2027 payment rates came in nearly flat and included a plan to stop counting diagnoses from unlinked chart reviews. UnitedHealth fell 20.7% and Humana 22% in the two days that followed, according to Morningstar. The CRUSH rule adds a backward-looking risk. If extrapolated audits survive, insurers could owe repayments calculated across years of contracts rather than a handful of sampled patients.

Our read: The clinic is where diagnoses get documented. If the extra revenue from documenting sicker patients shrinks, so does the return on a primary care center whose expansion case rested partly on that revenue. The strongest clinics, with full patient panels and good outcomes, should hold up. The marginal ones, opened quickly to build market share, are the most exposed.

The pullback has already started

The sector’s first retreat came before this week’s rule. In October 2025, CVS Health took a $5.7 billion goodwill impairment largely tied to Oak Street Health, the senior primary care chain it bought for $10.6 billion in 2023. It said it would close 16 underperforming clinics, about 7% of the footprint, by the end of February 2026 and would not open any new centers this year. A CVS spokesperson told Becker’s that the company was navigating elevated medical costs, CMS risk adjustment model changes and health plan payer dynamics. Some of the affected sites were barely broken in. An Oak Street clinic in Erie, Pennsylvania, that opened in 2024 had closed by May, the USA Today Network reported.

Sixteen clinics is not a wave. But it shows how quickly a value-based care operator can shift from growth to triage once the payment math changes, and Oak Street is not the only chain whose expansion plans were built on assumptions that are now under review.

What landlords should be asking

Healthcare tenants have been one of the most reliable demand stories in both retail and medical office. Medical outpatient building occupancy sits above 92%, according to Real Assets Adviser, and shopping center owners have spent years courting clinics for their long leases and daytime traffic. Those spaces are also expensive to create. Brokers quoted by WealthManagement.com have estimated that medical build-outs cost 40% to 50% more than traditional retail.

None of that demand is going away. Seniors still need primary care, and the aging population that drew insurers into the business is still aging. But the proposal changes the questions owners should ask about tenants whose revenue depends on Medicare Advantage.

The first is who actually stands behind the lease. A lease guaranteed by a Fortune 100 parent reads very differently from one signed by a clinic-level entity or a joint venture. The second is how each location performs on its own, since underperforming sites are the first to go when a chain consolidates, as Oak Street’s closures showed. Local market concentration matters too. A clinic in a county where one insurer dominates primary care carries more exposure to that insurer’s strategy than one competing in a crowded market. And the build-out itself is a risk. Specialized medical improvements can be costly to re-lease to a different user if a clinic goes dark, which makes the remaining lease term and the strength of the guarantee even more important.

What comes next

The rule is far from final. Comments are due Jan. 19, 2027. A federal judge in Texas vacated the previous version of the extrapolation rule in September 2025 after Humana sued, and the Fifth Circuit heard the government’s appeal in October. Insurers have also historically won concessions between proposed and final payment rules, and they will lobby hard on this one.

Even so, the direction of policy has been consistent for most of this year: tighter payment rates, closer scrutiny of coding and now the threat of retroactive repayment. Insurers are already adjusting their own real estate. Humana, which is working to restore profitability in its Medicare Advantage business, will require select employees to work from nine hub offices starting in 2027. The clinics on retail and medical office rent rolls deserve the same kind of scrutiny from the landlords who house them. A healthcare tenant is only as stable as the reimbursement model behind it.

item.title: Institutional Capital Discovers RV Parks as Consolidation Play Accelerates
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Brookfield invests $110 million in Open Road Resorts to roll up independent campgrounds, as institutions eye outdoor hospitality consolidation opportunities.

The post Institutional Capital Discovers RV Parks as Consolidation Play Accelerates appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Brookfield Asset Management agreed to buy a minority stake in Open Road Resorts for $110 million, funding the company’s acquisition of additional campgrounds across the United States. Open Road, which operates 14 properties including sites near Yellowstone National Park and in New York’s Finger Lakes region, plans to use the capital to continue rolling up independent campgrounds. Representatives for both Brookfield and Open Road declined to comment on the transaction.

Chase Becker and Jim Omstrom, former Citadel analysts, founded Open Road in 2019 and raised capital in 2024 from L Catterton and RV-maker Thor Industries. The company’s strategy centers on acquiring RV parks, upgrading facilities, and improving booking and revenue management systems. Its portfolio includes Raccoon Mountain campground near Chattanooga, Tennessee, and Rustic Timbers in Wisconsin’s Door County, with properties offering RV sites, glamping tents, and cabins for both transient and seasonal guests.

Brookfield’s investment comes as institutional investors increasingly view outdoor hospitality—including Airstream hotels and RV storage—as an attractive asset class. While Equity LifeStyle Properties and Sun Communities dominate the industry’s larger operators, the vast majority of U.S. RV parks remain owned by small operators. The pandemic drove demand for outdoor lodging, and Brookfield’s bet suggests institutional capital views the category as offering consolidation opportunities beyond short-term travel trends.

item.title: Major Employers Revive Office Footprint Through Hub-Based Return Plans
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Humana will require certain employees to work from nine hub offices starting in 2027, part of a phased return-to-office initiative.

The post Major Employers Revive Office Footprint Through Hub-Based Return Plans appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Humana will require select employees to work from designated offices at least three days per week starting in early 2027. The mandate applies only to workers living within 45 minutes of one of nine hub cities—Louisville, Arlington, Virginia, Boston, Chicago, Dallas, Fort Lauderdale, Florida, Nashville, Tennessee, New York, and Tampa, Florida—and whose roles are deemed to benefit from in-person collaboration. No relocations will be required, but future hiring for office-based positions will concentrate in these hubs.

The phased rollout begins in early 2027 with vice presidents and above, expands to directors and above in late 2027 and early 2028, and continues through 2028 with additional roles and locations. The company expects only a small percentage of its 65,000-employee workforce to be affected. Humana maintains a local workforce of roughly 10,000 in greater Louisville and 9,085 statewide, contributing nearly $13 billion in area economic activity according to an October report by University of Louisville economist Thomas Lambert.

The move follows October workforce cuts and comes as Humana works to restore profitability in its Medicare Advantage business. The company raised its full-year adjusted earnings outlook to at least $9.50 per share this month, citing better cost performance. The hub strategy reflects a broader shift among large employers moving away from blanket remote policies toward selective in-office requirements tied to specific roles and locations, a pattern that has implications for office space planning and regional labor markets.

Humana to Mandate Office Work for Select Louisville Staff

item.title: Machine Learning Is Finding More Signal in the Sensors Buildings Already Have
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Machine learning turns existing motion sensors and booking data into privacy-friendly occupancy insights for smarter, more efficient buildings.

The post Machine Learning Is Finding More Signal in the Sensors Buildings Already Have appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Most buildings generate a steady stream of occupancy information without producing much understanding. A badge swipe records that someone entered. A door contact records that it opened. A motion sensor records that something moved. Each of those is a binary event with a timestamp attached, and the picture they assemble is thin. A space either registered activity or it did not.

Operators who want more than that have generally been told to buy more hardware, usually cameras with computer vision or dense arrays of specialized sensors. Both work. Both are expensive, and cameras bring privacy objections that many tenants and employees are not willing to accept regardless of how the footage gets handled.

Research published last November suggests a third option that uses equipment buildings already have. A team from Malmö University’s Sustainable Digitalisation Research Centre worked with data from seven meeting rooms outfitted with two inexpensive passive infrared motion sensors apiece, one positioned at the door and one covering the room interior. Neither sensor counts anything. Each one reports only whether it detected movement during a short interval.

What the researchers added was the room booking calendar and a set of machine learning models trained to find patterns in how those binary signals arrive. Rather than treating each sensor trigger as an isolated event, the models looked at the relationships between them, including how much time passed between door events, how many interior motion events occurred during that window, the average interval between those motions, the longest quiet stretch, and how many door events happened before and after. Room dimensions, seating capacity, day of week, and time of day all went in as well.

The resulting estimates were considerably better than what a motion sensor on its own can produce. The best-performing model landed within one person of the true headcount 68.5 percent of the time during occupied periods and within two people 81.6 percent of the time. Adding the booking calendar improved accuracy by about four percentage points. Exact headcounts remained difficult, with accuracy around 39 percent, which the authors attribute to treating each sensor activation in isolation rather than as part of a sequence.

Knowing whether four or five people are in a twelve-seat room is enough to drive HVAC zoning, room recommendations, and space planning. It is not enough for headcount during an evacuation, and the authors are clear that they are not proposing it for that.

Some of the more interesting findings had nothing to do with counting. Across the data set, rooms sat unoccupied 87.6 percent of recorded time, and during standard office hours only about a third were in use. Nearly a third of booked time involved rooms that nobody occupied, while almost 30 percent of actual occupancy happened in rooms that were never booked. Meetings started late roughly a third of the time and ended early slightly more often than that. Eighty-eight percent of bookings were made by groups smaller than the room’s seating capacity, and the most common difference between estimated occupancy and available seats ran between four and ten empty chairs.

Any office manager would recognize those behaviors. Very few have been able to quantify them, and quantifying them is what turns an observation into a budget argument.

The appeal of working with existing infrastructure extends past the hardware savings. Passive infrared sensors are already installed throughout most commercial buildings for lighting control and HVAC, which means the marginal cost of this approach is software rather than installation. A sensor that detects motion and reports nothing about who produced it also sidesteps the privacy conversation entirely, which matters for anyone who has tried to introduce camera-based analytics into an occupied floor.

For building engineers, estimated headcounts rather than binary presence changes what mechanical systems can respond to. Conditioning a twelve-person conference room for twelve people when three are present wastes energy on a schedule that repeats daily across a portfolio. Office managers get a picture of which rooms get booked but not used, which sizes actually get filled, and which teams consistently reserve more space than they need. Designers working on a repositioning have evidence about how a floor plate performs rather than assumptions carried over from the last project.

There is also a design question running the other direction, which is how to configure space so these inferences get easier. Rooms with a single clear entry point produce cleaner passage data than those with multiple doors. Sensor placement that avoids counting people who linger in a doorway without entering reduces false triggers. Furniture arrangements that keep occupants within a motion sensor’s field of view prevent the system from reading a seated meeting as an empty room. Booking systems that require a check-in produce calendar data that actually corresponds to reality, which is where the Malmö researchers found the weakest link in their own inputs.

The researchers point toward sequence-aware models as the next step, since architectures built to recognize patterns across time would likely handle exact counting better than the approach they tested. Whether that closes the distance to camera-level accuracy is unresolved. What the current results suggest is that buildings have been generating more usable information than anyone was extracting from it, and the equipment to capture it was installed years ago.

The post Machine Learning Is Finding More Signal in the Sensors Buildings Already Have appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Section 8 Suspension Lists Fail to Catch Chicago Landlords Before Collapse
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Chicago Housing Authority's voucher suspension list often flags distressed landlords only after foreclosures hit, while single-asset LLCs let investors sidestep bans.

The post Section 8 Suspension Lists Fail to Catch Chicago Landlords Before Collapse appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Chicago Housing Authority maintains a suspension list barring landlords from new Housing Choice Voucher contracts when they fail inspections, collect payments on empty units, or violate building codes. Since 2018, the agency has issued 433 suspensions against 402 landlord companies and individuals, with 246 still active as of October. Four out-of-state investors—Yissocher Rotenberg, Chaim Bialostozky, Mark Nussbaum and Eliazer Tauber—accounted for roughly 30 percent of large multifamily foreclosure filings in Chicago in 2025, with lenders seeking at least $87 million. Three of the four appear on CHA’s suspension roster, but often only after their properties deteriorated.

CHA suspends individual LLCs rather than the people controlling them, allowing the same investor to draw voucher subsidies at one building while barred at another. Chaim Bialostozky faced foreclosure suits from Fannie Mae and Walker & Dunlop totaling more than $44 million before CHA suspended two of his entities in August and September 2026. Straightline Management, run by Jacob Tauber and managing buildings bought by his father Eliazer Tauber and Mark Nussbaum, was suspended in May 2024 for contract violations; the ban remained in effect more than two years later. CHA can extend suspensions across an entire portfolio when it discovers landlords using multiple vendor IDs to avoid sanctions, but enforcement varies case by case.

The suspension list includes 241 contract violations since 2019, most for failed inspections or skipped training, and 19 for collecting payments on vacant units. Stuart Handler’s TLC Management saw 1,009 units affected before its suspension lifted in July 2025, while some operators report suspensions resolved within weeks. CHA cross-references the city’s problem landlord and building code scofflaw lists quarterly. Investors targeting voucher holders as tenants created a reliable revenue stream, but the structure of single-asset LLCs and inconsistent enforcement means suspensions often trail foreclosures and tenant safety risks rather than prevent them.

The Real Deal
Chicago Has an Early Alarm System for Multifamily Distress. Why Didn’t the Bell Ring?

item.title: Office Trends Are Pointing Toward Faster Reconfiguration and Peak Day Capacity
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Office leasing trends for 2027 show tenants choosing fewer, higher-quality spaces, flexible layouts, smarter data and peak-day performance.

The post Office Trends Are Pointing Toward Faster Reconfiguration and Peak Day Capacity appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Office leasing decisions used to follow a fairly predictable formula, with headcount driving square footage and long leases locking in the result. That formula has loosened considerably. Hybrid schedules have settled into patterns that vary by company and by team, AI is changing which work happens in person, and business plans are being revised more often than most leases allow.

Those shifts came up repeatedly during a recent Propmodo webinar on office market trends and portfolio strategies heading into 2027. Panelists described occupiers who are being more deliberate about where they invest and more demanding about how their space performs.

Peter Miscovich, Executive Managing Director and Global Future of Work Leader at JLL, said many of his corporate clients are concentrating their real estate budgets into fewer locations and spending more on each one, with the goal of supporting innovation and attracting talent. “There’s more selectivity and prioritization. Most of my clients are looking at fewer sites with greater investments per square foot,” he said. “They want better outcomes for those fewer sites, especially for things like innovation and talent attraction. The good old days of increasing your portfolio size with your headcount, that is being decoupled.”

Bringing more people into fewer offices raises the stakes on the busiest days of the week. Thierry Ondet, Managing Director at ROOM, said the measure of a good office is how it holds up at peak attendance, and many customers still run into problems there. “I would say that what defines quality today is whether or not I use the space on a busy Tuesday,” he said. “I still hear from customers telling us that they struggle to find a space where they can make a private phone call or book a meeting room on the busiest days.”

At Kastle Systems, Chief Product Officer Todd Burner has watched clients move away from blanket attendance requirements toward policies focused on which employees are in the office together. Law firms, in particular, want junior associates present when senior associates are there to teach them. “The law firms that we work with are very focused on who are the people in the office, because the junior associate needs to learn from the experience of the senior associates,” he said. “I think we’re seeing a lot more focus on making sure that the right people are in at the right times, and not just saying we want four days for four days’ sake.”

Miscovich said corporate real estate guidelines have become more flexible to support that kind of calibration, giving local offices room to adjust and allowing those adjustments to happen quickly. “The guidelines are becoming more flexible and give each office a lot of room to change for what the local office environment calls for,” he said. “These localized changes are happening faster and faster, sometimes as quickly as three months or even every 30 days.”

ROOM’s customers are asking for their floors to change on a similar timeline, according to Ondet, who said a traditional build-out is too slow for many of them. “A lot of our customers want to have the ability to really reconfigure the space very quickly,” he said. “And very quickly, it’s not in a matter of six months or a year and doing a build-out, but it’s really within sometimes a matter of weeks to reorganize the space.”

Making impactful changes depends on understanding how the space is being used. AI is helping empower office managers and designers to know much more context about how space is being used without accidentally stepping into privacy concerns. “I think we’re going to find a way to better understand what people are doing in the office in a way that doesn’t compromise individual privacy,” he said. “Once we do that we will be able to tell occupiers how their office is performing at a segment level or at a group level that really helps them and their building managers understand how they are consuming space.”

Across the discussion, panelists described occupiers that are committing to fewer locations, measuring space by how it holds up on peak days, adjusting workplace policies every few months and expecting floors that can be reconfigured in weeks. They also pointed to a growing need for usage data that helps tenants and building managers understand how space is consumed without tracking individuals.

Those expectations are taking shape in a market where demand is recovering while supply keeps shrinking. The U.S. office market recorded its fifth consecutive quarter of positive net absorption in Q3, with 6.0 million square feet of occupancy gains and 21 million square feet year to date, according to JLL. Only 3.5 million square feet of new office space was completed during the quarter, while 9.6 million square feet was removed from inventory, and total inventory has fallen by more than 45 million square feet since late 2023, JLL reports. Peak days are already testing the best buildings, with Class A+ properties reaching 94.8% occupancy on Tuesday, October 27, according to Kastle. With demand rising and few new options coming online, we may see buildings that can handle those busy days, adapt quickly and give tenants useful data on how their space performs capture a larger share of the leasing activity ahead.

item.title: Builder’s Remedy Provision Faces Court Test in Menlo Park High-Rise Fight
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
A lawsuit over a 39-story Menlo Park tower could determine whether California cities must approve Builder's Remedy projects that exceed local zoning.

The post Builder’s Remedy Provision Faces Court Test in Menlo Park High-Rise Fight appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
A developer is using California’s Builder’s Remedy provision to push a 665-unit mixed-use project through Menlo Park over local objections. N17 Development filed suit in October seeking $6.65 million in fines against the city for refusing to approve Willow Park, a complex that would include a 39-story residential tower, offices, a hotel, and retail on a nearly seven-acre parcel. California Attorney General Rob Bonta warned the city in July to approve the project or face penalties under state housing law. Menlo Park became subject to the Builder’s Remedy after missing a January 2023 deadline to submit a compliant housing plan, which the city blames on administrative delays in Sacramento.

Developer Oisin Heneghan argues the project addresses Silicon Valley’s housing shortage and would set aside 15 percent of units as affordable, with two-bedroom units renting for $2,556 monthly in an area near Meta’s headquarters and Stanford University. Menlo Park officials say they want environmental reviews before approving construction, particularly regarding impacts on a creek that hosts steelhead and the California red-legged frog. Local opponents also cite the property owner: an entity controlled by Vitaly Yusufov, son of a former Russian energy minister, though his attorney says he is a real estate developer with European projects and no Kremlin connections. U.S. Rep. Sam Liccardo asked the Treasury Department in September to review the project on national-security grounds.

Neighboring Palo Alto plans to file a brief supporting Menlo Park, with one city councilman saying an adverse ruling would force cities to approve Builder’s Remedy projects. Pro-housing advocates counter that aggressive enforcement is necessary given California’s housing crisis. The case could define how much control cities retain over development when they fall out of compliance with state housing mandates, particularly regarding local height limits that the Builder’s Remedy allows developers to bypass.

The Silicon Valley Brawl Over a 39-Story Tower in a Leafy Suburban Neighborhood

item.title: Leaseback Structures Now Back Nearly Half of US Data Center Construction
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Hyperscalers are becoming tenants in their own data centers

The post Leaseback Structures Now Back Nearly Half of US Data Center Construction appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
2 days 24 hr agoNov. 16, 2026 5:20 pm

Ownership of the AI buildout is quietly separating from the companies doing the building. Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust agreed last week to acquire a majority stake in a data center portfolio from Amazon in a deal valued around $5 billion, taking 75.1 percent of two joint ventures holding 13 newly built powered shells across campuses in Indiana and Mississippi. Amazon Web Services keeps 24.9 percent, worth about $600 million, and leases back the entire portfolio on an initial 12-year term extending to 32 years if fully exercised. The portfolio carries 647 megawatts and priced at a 7 percent initial capitalization rate. BXDC funded it with roughly $1.9 billion of proceeds from the public offering it completed earlier this year plus about $2.5 billion in new non-recourse mortgage debt.

Amazon’s reason for selling buildings it intends to keep using is visible in its own disclosures. The company raised 2026 cash capital expenditure guidance to roughly $220 billion in July, up from $200 billion, which Andy Jassy attributed largely to higher memory costs, and held that figure steady at third-quarter earnings. Trailing twelve-month free cash flow swung to an outflow of $42.4 billion by the end of the third quarter, against a $14.8 billion inflow a year earlier, as trailing capital expenditure reached roughly $211 billion versus $168.3 billion of operating cash flow. Cash capital expenditures in the quarter alone were $75.9 billion.

Jassy has been direct about the timing problem underneath those numbers, noting that data center capital goes out roughly two years before the servers inside produce revenue and that free cash flow headwinds continue until the sites are monetized. AWS carries a backlog around $496 billion and grew 39 percent in the quarter, so the constraint is not demand. It is the lag between writing the check and collecting the rent, and a sale-leaseback shortens that considerably by converting a finished building into cash while keeping the capacity.

Meta has run the same play at larger scale and pioneered the template. Its Hyperion campus in Richland Parish, Louisiana, sits inside a special purpose vehicle managed by Blue Owl Capital that raised roughly $27 billion in external debt, with Meta holding 20 percent as minority partner and tenant and providing residual value guarantees near $28 billion. Meta announced a similar venture with BlackRock in El Paso at roughly $14 billion for a one-gigawatt campus, again taking 20 percent alongside the land and about $2.3 billion of construction. A third Texas venture followed at comparable size, returning $1.04 billion in cash to Meta.

The aggregate obligation created by all of this is now large enough that ratings agencies have started tracking it separately. Moody’s calculated that the five largest US hyperscalers held $969 billion in undiscounted future data center lease commitments at the end of 2025, with $662 billion sitting off balance sheet because the leases had not yet commenced. Later tallies put the uncommenced figure above $1 trillion, with Microsoft carrying the largest disclosed pipeline. The Bank for International Settlements described the mechanics in its March Quarterly Review as substituting upfront capital expenditure for multi-year operating expenses financed through dedicated vehicles backed by private credit.

Sizing the leaseback share against total development requires some estimation, since nobody publishes a clean tally. The Census Bureau put private US data center construction at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of about $85 billion in August, up 73 percent year over year, against $49.7 billion for all of 2025. The announced joint venture and leaseback structures over roughly the past eighteen months, counting Hyperion, El Paso, the second Texas venture, and now the AWS portfolio, total somewhere near $60 billion. Measured against perhaps $125 billion of US data center construction put in place over the same window, that suggests close to half the capital behind the largest projects is now arriving through structures where the operator is a tenant rather than an owner. The figure is imprecise and heavily weighted toward Meta, but the direction is not ambiguous.

Development economics change when the end buyer is identified before the slab is poured. A hyperscaler building for its own account underwrites against internal cost of capital and holds whatever it builds. A hyperscaler building for contribution to a venture underwrites against what a Blackstone or a Blue Owl will pay, which means cap rates, lease terms, and residual value assumptions start shaping design decisions the way they already do in industrial and net lease. The 7 percent cap rate on the AWS portfolio is a real number that other developers can price against, and the 12-year initial term with a 32-year extension is a real duration that lenders can underwrite.

What remains unresolved is who holds the risk when a 12-year lease expires on a building designed for hardware that turns over every four or five years. Powered shells age better than the equipment inside them, which is most of the argument for this asset class, but the residual value guarantees Meta attached to its ventures suggest the capital partners wanted something more than that argument. We would expect more of these transactions in 2027 given how much construction is still in the pipeline and how thin free cash flow has become across the group, and we would watch the guarantee terms more closely than the headline prices.

The post Leaseback Structures Now Back Nearly Half of US Data Center Construction appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Geothermal Drilling Gains Traction as Data Centers Hunt Grid Capacity
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Bedrock Energy raised $24 million to expand geothermal drilling for commercial buildings and data centers seeking grid capacity relief.

The post Geothermal Drilling Gains Traction as Data Centers Hunt Grid Capacity appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Bedrock Energy closed a $24 million funding round to expand its AI-directed geothermal drilling operation for commercial buildings. The startup uses directional drilling techniques adapted from oil and gas extraction to install geothermal heat pump systems up to 1,000 feet deep. Bedrock claims its rigs cut drilling time by up to 80% compared to conventional water-well-style equipment, reducing installation costs for systems that use the earth as a year-round heat source and sink. The company currently operates in Texas, Utah, Colorado, New York, and Alberta.

Clean Energy Ventures and Clearvision Ventures led the round, joined by GVP Climate, Susquehanna Sustainable Investments, Catalytic Capital for Climate and Health by Temasek Trust, and several other investors. Bedrock raised $12 million in its Series A last year and $8.5 million in a 2023 seed round. The new capital will fund rig purchases and expansion into New England, New Jersey, the upper Midwest, and additional Western states. The company has drilled nine sites to date and secured commitments from customers planning installations over the next two years.

Data center developers have emerged as a customer segment alongside office and commercial properties. Some operators want geothermal cooling for server racks, but others see the technology as a way to free up grid capacity by deploying it on adjacent parcels. CEO Joselyn Lai said one Michigan prospect estimated that freeing a few megawatts could accelerate data center operations by months or a full year. Geothermal heat pumps require minimal maintenance once installed, making them attractive for long-term infrastructure projects where upfront costs can be amortized over decades of service.

Tech Crunch

item.title: Phoenix Midtown Gets Corporate Anchor as U-Haul Fills Distressed Tower
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
U-Haul consolidates 2,000 employees in a Phoenix tower bought from foreclosure, stabilizing a distressed midtown asset as the office market recovers selectively.

The post Phoenix Midtown Gets Corporate Anchor as U-Haul Fills Distressed Tower appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
U-Haul has moved 2,000 employees into a 25-story office tower at 20 East Thomas Road in Phoenix, completing its acquisition and renovation of the former CenturyLink building. The company paid $23.7 million for the 548,938-square-foot property in December 2024, two years after the building entered foreclosure through lender Second Step Asset Management, a Bank of America affiliate. The building was 84% vacant at acquisition. Only one tenant remains: HDR Engineering, which occupies 20,000 square feet and is negotiating to double its footprint.

U-Haul expanded from roughly 300,000 square feet in its previous Central Avenue headquarters to 500,000 square feet in the new building. CEO Joe Shoen said the company needed room to grow after filling all 22 floors of its original two-tower complex, where it had operated since relocating from Portland in 1967. The company retained ownership of its former headquarters and surrounding parcels between Central Avenue and 3rd Street, including a conference center and fitness facility that opened in 2021. Shoen said the old towers may be repurposed for self-storage or nonprofit office space, though no final plans have been set.

U-Haul employs nearly 4,000 people in Arizona and maintains a market capitalization above $10.6 billion. The company reported $137 million in earnings for its second fiscal quarter of 2027, up from $106 million the prior year, driven by self-storage and its U-Box portable container service, which together account for 25% of revenue. Self-storage revenue has grown 71% since the second quarter of fiscal 2022.

Phoenix office vacancy stood at 22% in the third quarter of 2026, down from 24% the prior year, but midtown Phoenix posted a 26.7% vacancy rate that has trended higher even as the broader market recovered. Midtown asking rents average 15% below market, with Class A buildings in top submarkets commanding nearly double midtown rates. CoStar analysts said the submarket is positioned to attract tenants seeking quality towers at discounted pricing, a profile U-Haul’s occupancy validates.
